title: Best starting point for making a playable game with AI, Claude?
author: 3eyedstudio
selftext: ​I’ve been lurking here for a couple of weeks and have been blown away by the games you’re all making. While I’ve used AI to generate images before, I’ve never actually used it to start building a playable game. I see tons of awesome showcases, but not much about the actual workflow or how people get off the ground. I’d really appreciate it if anyone could share their process or point me in the right direction to get started!

comments.author: MelodramaticShape
comments.body: There is no one "correct" way. Just start prompting, find out the limitations for yourself. You could get some playable slop in a single prompt. If you want an actual production ready game it's going to take a lot of trial and error.

replies.author: 3eyedstudio
replies.body: I understand that, I guess it seems daunting to  dive into this. I haven't even tried Claude yet. I've primarily been using gemini, and Ive been seeing people creating amazing things through claude. thanks for the tip.

comments.author: Swimming_Iron_619
comments.body:
Download Godot. Create new project. Open that folder in Claude.

It's that simple. Start prompting claude, it'll see it's a godot project. 

Start with something small. Don't give it the full game in 1 prompt. You can give context for what you want so it knows how / why it's building it but just make little steps and test often.

replies.author: 3eyedstudio
replies.body: thank you this really helps,  I just need a starting point. appreciate it!

replies.author: Ferniclestix
replies.body:
step 1 though, get claude to build its own set of tests for performance and frame rate.  

then have a discussion with it about your project and ask it to build a project document and set out a kind of to do or wish list of things you want.   
then go step by step.    
performance checks, main menu, settings, controls.

start on gameplay when you are ready but be sure to define things in very specific terms. if you must makea glossary of things so that you both know what you are talking about when you refer to something.

one other important thing is ask claude to keep things organised into smaller files based on functions and not to use 'monolithic files'

this reduces errors hugely and will result in much cleaner code.

comments.author: ArtificialBeingsInc
comments.body: One concrete first project in Godot: move a square around a room, collect a circle, show a win message, then restart. Ask Claude for one piece at a time and run the scene after each. Save a working copy before the next change; if something breaks, tell it what you did, what happened, and the first debugger error if there is one. Placeholder shapes are plenty until the loop works.

comments.author: Just-Routine967
comments.body:
Make sure you explain the scope/systems you are wanting in your intial prompt so you don't have to rework code because the quick easy implementation it chose to give you your prototype can't achieve the final goal.

Usually I start with a pretty detailed design document, the less you make it guess what you want the better. Then I'll have one agent begin on the framework and another create a visual mockup which I usually work with to refine the look I want while the first agent is implementing the mechanical side. 
Once the look is finalized the first agent just requests whatever assets or visual effects it needs for to tie in with the phase it's working through, and I playtest at the end of each phase.

comments.author: phiiiiiiii
comments.body: Get a $20 Claude Code subscription, then ask it to build a baseline folder for your game. It will ask you what you want to set up, but generally you should start with Godot and go from there.
